strengths: The manuscript addresses a timely evaluation gap: joint text-to-audio-video systems require assessment of visual quality, audio quality, synchronization, instruction following, and realism rather than isolated unimodal metrics. The 500-prompt suite combines 400 curated prompts with 100 prompts inverted from real videos and targets challenging phenomena such as overlapping sounds, off-screen audio, multi-event narratives, and physical interactions. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/7b0d2770cbac4f0d90b31e405605a937/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The taxonomy is broad and diagnostically useful. It decomposes instruction following into 17 sub-dimensions and realism into temporal coherence, object integrity, motion smoothness, acoustic artifacts, and material–timbre consistency. The checklist prompts and scoring rubrics in the appendix make the intended evaluation procedure relatively transparent.

The empirical comparison covers 11 systems, including open and proprietary end-to-end models and two composed pipelines. Fine-grained tables expose heterogeneous strengths that would be hidden by a single aggregate score; for example, the composed Wan-2.2 plus Hunyuan-Foley system leads video realism while end-to-end systems generally perform better on instruction following.

The paper is generally readable and visually well organized. It also acknowledges judge bias, computational expense, and incomplete long-tail coverage; these are appropriate limitations rather than reasons by themselves to penalize the work.
weaknesses: The central MLLM-as-a-judge methodology is not validated against human judgments. The paper reports no human annotation protocol, sample size, inter-rater agreement, judge–human correlation, pairwise ranking accuracy, calibration study, or comparison across judge models. Deterministic decoding does not establish validity. Because all subjective results and the claimed audio-realism bottleneck depend on a single Gemini-2.5-Pro judge, this omission is a fundamental soundness problem.

The claim that models remain below “human-level realism” is unsupported: no human-created-video baseline or human performance is reported in Tables 2–3. Although the appendix describes real YouTube clips as a realism ceiling, their scores never appear. Likewise, comparing video- and audio-realism numbers does not by itself prove an audio bottleneck because the two dimensions use different rubrics whose scales have not been calibrated.

The model comparison is not controlled fairly. Outputs use different resolutions, including 480p, 720p, and 1080p, while technical and aesthetic metrics are resolution-sensitive. Moreover, only Ovi-1.1 and the composed pipelines receive Gemini-paraphrased prompts, so systems are not evaluated on identical inputs. Native frame rates, sampling rates, durations, and potentially other generation settings also vary without a normalization or sensitivity analysis.

There is no uncertainty analysis despite stochastic generation and judging. The manuscript does not state the number of generations or random seeds per prompt, report confidence intervals, test statistical significance, or quantify repeated-judge variance. Small differences in the ranking tables therefore cannot be interpreted reliably.

Several metric choices and aggregation procedures are underspecified or insufficiently justified. The exact Audiobox PQ/CU implementations, checkpoints, preprocessing, and normalization are absent; the applicability of Synchformer to arbitrary open-domain events is not established; the subset used for the talking-face LatentSync score is unclear; and missing scores are unexplained. The conversion from 1–5 judge ratings to reported percentages, treatment of null checklist items, weighting across prompts/sub-dimensions, and construction of the four-way average are also not defined.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a benchmark submission. The supplied manuscript does not provide an accessible dataset/code release, and the section claiming to present all prompts contains only prompt-engineering templates. Initial corpus sizes, clustering algorithm, sampling counts, audit annotator numbers, adjudication procedures, agreement, model/API versions, access dates, generation parameters, and objective-evaluator configurations are missing.

Dataset-quality evidence is weak. “Semantic retention rate” is not defined and embedding-space distinctiveness alone does not demonstrate meaningful coverage. There is no audit of generated checklists for correctness or completeness. There are also internal inconsistencies: real clips are described as 4–10 seconds in the main text but 5–10 seconds in the appendix, and the listed thematic percentages total 120%.

Ethical and legal treatment is missing. The benchmark uses prompts from online communities and 100 YouTube clips, but does not discuss licenses, consent/privacy, redistribution rights, demographic representation, harmful-content filtering beyond a figure label, or the implications of evaluating proprietary services. These issues are material if the videos, captions, or prompts are to be released.

Originality is moderate rather than strong: combining established signal metrics with checklist-based MLLM judging is useful, but closely overlaps the stated scope of benchmarks such as VABench and JavisBench. The “first comprehensive benchmark” claim is not convincingly substantiated, and the empirical analysis is mostly descriptive. Presentation also needs proofreading, with malformed spacing, duplicated Table 4 numbering, inconsistent model capitalization, and several grammatical errors. Overall, the promising taxonomy does not compensate for the missing validation of the central evaluator and the uncontrolled comparison protocol.

strengths: Significance: Evaluating joint text-to-audio-video generation is timely, and the taxonomy covers useful dimensions spanning visual quality, audio quality, synchronization, instruction following, and realism.

Scope: The evaluation includes 11 end-to-end and composed systems, including both open and proprietary models, and reports reasonably detailed per-dimension results rather than only a single leaderboard score.

Presentation: The benchmark construction pipeline, taxonomies, scoring rubrics, and judge prompts are extensively documented in the appendices. The main tables are generally readable and expose several plausible model failure patterns.
Limitations: The paper appropriately acknowledges MLLM bias, evaluation cost, limited long-tail coverage, and the need for future human feedback.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central MLLM-as-judge methodology receives essentially no validation against human judgments. There are no expert annotations, inter-rater agreement measurements, judge-human correlations, judge-model ablations, repeated evaluations, or sensitivity analyses. Appendix B explicitly relegates human-in-the-loop validation to future work. Consequently, the instruction-following and realism scores—and especially the claimed “Audio Realism Bottleneck”—are not presently trustworthy.

Soundness: The abstract claims that models fall short of “human-level realism,” and Appendix F describes the real-video subset as a “realism ceiling,” but no human or real-video baseline appears in the reported results. This important conclusion is therefore unsupported.

Soundness: The evaluation uses Gemini-2.5-Pro both to enrich/caption benchmark prompts and to construct and score checklist items. This creates substantial shared-model and stylistic bias, yet the paper does not test alternative prompt generators or judges. Reasoning-first output alone is not evidence of scoring accuracy or robustness.

Soundness: Each sub-dimension is reduced to at most one automatically generated binary question, despite prompts averaging 154 tokens and 3.61 events. This can discard many constraints and conflicts with the claim of granular, comprehensive instruction evaluation. The paper provides no audit of checklist correctness, completeness, or ambiguity.

Experimental fairness: Systems are evaluated at different native resolutions and potentially different durations/settings; Kling is run at 1080p, most systems at 720p, and Javis at 480p, although technical-quality metrics are then compared directly. More seriously, prompts are paraphrased only for Ovi-1.1 and the composed pipelines, so models do not receive identical semantic inputs. No controlled comparison establishes that these choices are equitable.

Metrics: Several adopted metrics are insufficiently specified or justified for this setting. The exact Audiobox PQ/CU evaluators and checkpoints are not identified; DOVER++ is described as applied to “representative frames” without a reproducible sampling procedure; Synchformer and LatentSync apply only to restricted synchronization regimes; and the validity of ImageBind similarity for fine-grained audiovisual correspondence is not established. No metric-human correlation study is provided.

Statistical evidence: Results are presented almost entirely as point estimates. There are no confidence intervals, per-prompt variance, significance tests, bootstrap comparisons, or analysis of API stochasticity. It is therefore unclear which model differences are meaningful, particularly the small gaps in Tables 2 and 3.

Reproducibility: The paper omits important generation details such as exact API/model versions or access dates, seeds, number of generations per prompt, failure/retry handling, duration normalization, and complete preprocessing and aggregation procedures. Appendix G is labeled as presenting all prompts but actually contains rewriting, extraction, and judging templates rather than the 500 benchmark prompts. No accessible code, data artifact, generated outputs, checklist annotations, or YouTube URL/timestamp list is supplied in the manuscript.

Originality: The work combines established signal metrics, embedding similarities, and an MLLM judge over a new prompt set. Relative to JavisBench and VABench, the main novelty is the taxonomy and added realism rubrics; the strong “first comprehensive benchmark” claim is not convincingly supported by the related-work comparison.

Presentation: Some terminology and interpretation are inconsistent. For example, AAS is variously described as acoustic artifacts and “Audio-Visual Artifacts,” while the discussion of Sora-2's lower AAS incorrectly interprets it as fine-grained attribute adherence. Numerous grammatical and typesetting issues further reduce precision.

Ethics and data governance: Prompts and videos are collected from community platforms and YouTube, but licensing, creator consent, privacy/person filtering, redistribution rights, and demographic or cultural bias are not discussed. The diagram mentions an NSFW filter without specifying its implementation or error analysis. These omissions matter for a benchmark intended for release and reuse. strengths: Significance is high: unified evaluation of text-to-audio-video generation is timely, and the benchmark targets important shortcomings of unimodal evaluations, especially audio-video synchronization, compositional instruction following, and physical realism.

The 500-prompt suite is constructed around a useful taxonomy and includes difficult phenomena such as overlapping audio events, off-screen sources, multiple subjects, event chains, cinematographic constraints, and material-timbre consistency.

The evaluation is broad, covering 11 end-to-end and composed systems with both established signal-level metrics and fine-grained diagnostic dimensions. The breakdowns in Tables 2–4 expose meaningful differences that a single aggregate score would conceal.

The checklist-based instruction-following design and separate realism criteria are promising and reasonably interpretable. The appendix provides the QA-generation prompts, judge rubrics, deterministic decoding setting, frame-sampling rate, and synchronization search-window setting.

Presentation is generally clear and visually effective. The manuscript also honestly acknowledges evaluation cost, MLLM bias, and incomplete long-tail coverage; these limitations should not themselves be penalized.
weaknesses: The central soundness problem is the absence of human validation for the Gemini-2.5-Pro judge. There is no human correlation, agreement analysis, judge calibration, multi-judge comparison, or robustness study. Qualitative examples in Figure 4 cannot establish that the evaluator reliably measures instruction following, temporal coherence, acoustic artifacts, or material-timbre consistency. Consequently, Tables 3–4 and the claimed “Audio Realism Bottleneck” are not yet sufficiently supported.

The system comparison contains substantial confounds. Outputs use native resolutions and rates, including Javis at 480p, most models at 720p, and Kling at 1080p, although several quality metrics are resolution-sensitive. Moreover, prompts are paraphrased with Gemini only for Ovi-1.1 and the composed pipelines. This changes the tested instructions and undermines direct instruction-following comparisons.

Important aggregation and statistical details are missing: the paper does not explain handling of null checklist items, per-prompt weighting, normalization into the reported percentages, applicability filtering for synchronization and lip-sync metrics, or missing LS entries. It reports no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variability across generations, so many model-ranking differences may not be meaningful.

Several objective components are insufficiently specified or justified. Exact implementations and checkpoints for PQ and CU are unclear; keyframe selection is unspecified; ImageBind similarity measures semantic compatibility rather than temporal alignment; and the validity of applying Synchformer broadly to heterogeneous, multi-source scenes is not demonstrated. No comparison to human judgments verifies that this collection of metrics reflects audiovisual quality on this benchmark.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the included judge prompts. The manuscript does not enumerate the 500 benchmark prompts as claimed, clearly specify generation seeds and sample counts, record proprietary API versions/dates and complete parameters, or describe a concrete release package containing code, outputs, annotations, and evaluator checkpoints. Reproducing results for changing closed-source systems would therefore be difficult.

Dataset construction lacks annotation-quality evidence. The number and expertise of human auditors, audit instructions, adjudication process, inter-annotator agreement, and fraction manually checked are not reported. Claims of “superior semantic distinctiveness” are also made without a precise definition, uncertainty estimates, or a sufficiently controlled comparison.

Some claims are overstated or internally inconsistent. Calling this the “first comprehensive benchmark” is difficult to reconcile with the paper's own discussion of JavisBench and VABench. The abstract claims a shortfall from “human-level” realism, but no human ceiling appears in the reported experiments. Additionally, the seven thematic percentages in Appendix F.2 sum to 120%, indicating a reporting or categorization error that needs clarification.

The ethics discussion is insufficient for a benchmark drawing from YouTube UGC, community prompts, and generated human speech. The paper does not address licenses, creator consent, privacy or biometric content, copyrighted audio, takedown procedures, demographic representation, or the operational details of NSFW filtering. These are material release considerations, not merely generic limitations.

Overall, the benchmark idea is useful and potentially accept-worthy, but the unvalidated learned judge and confounded comparison directly affect its central empirical claims. Human validation, controlled generation settings, statistical analysis, and a concrete reproducibility and data-governance plan are needed before others can reliably build on the results.

strengths: The manuscript presents a timely and potentially useful benchmark for joint text-to-audio-video evaluation, with 500 prompts, 15 systems, and coverage of video quality, audio quality, cross-modal alignment, instruction following, and realism. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/d582f238b6cf44d684bd3a9422ff55d2/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The taxonomy targets meaningful failure modes that simpler unimodal benchmarks miss, including material-timbre consistency, object permanence, audiovisual synchronization, interactions, and unwanted speech.

The empirical scope is broad: the paper compares proprietary and open-source end-to-end systems with cascaded T2V-to-audio and audio-to-video pipelines, and reports useful fine-grained results rather than only a single leaderboard score.

The authors make several valuable validation attempts, including five-annotator studies, human pairwise comparisons, repeated judge runs, synchronization-metric validation, preprocessing sensitivity tests, and calibration on real videos.

Presentation is generally clear and visually effective, and the appendices disclose the prompt-rewriting, checklist-extraction, and judge prompts. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges judge bias, vendor drift, computational cost, and incomplete long-tail coverage.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not controlled fairly. Appendix F states that prompts are paraphrased with Gemini-2.5-Pro only for Ovi-1.1 and composed pipelines, while other systems receive the original prompts. This changes the evaluated instructions in a benchmark whose principal outcome is instruction following. Systems also use heterogeneous native resolutions, including 480p, 720p, and 1080p, directly confounding video-quality metrics. No controlled common-prompt/common-resolution analysis is reported.

The human-validation description is internally inconsistent. The paper says five annotators independently rated every one of 250 samples, which should produce 2,500 annotator pairs per dimension, but Equation 1 reports only 503 valid pairs. The missingness or assignment design is not explained. Moreover, Gemini-2.5-Pro differs from human consensus by about one Likert point for instruction following and 1.42 points for audio realism, the latter 36.3% worse than the inter-human baseline. This is substantial uncertainty for a leaderboard and for the headline audio-realism conclusion.

The claimed pairwise validation is incomplete in the appendix: only human-derived Elo scores and the human head-to-head matrix are shown, although the text asserts that Gemini reproduces the human ordering. The judge-derived matrix, scores, agreement statistics, and uncertainty are absent. The Elo conversion is also mathematically incorrect: with the stated Bradley-Terry model using exp(theta), defining Elo = 1500 + 400 theta does not make a 400-point gap correspond to a 90.9% win probability; it corresponds to about 73.1%.

Key aggregation rules are under-specified or problematic. The paper does not clearly explain treatment of null checklist dimensions, failed generations, or how the five realism metrics become the two reported realism scores. The IF-Audio equation can fall outside the claimed [0,1] range and leaves the speech score undefined when speech is not requested. The overall score is an unvalidated equal-weight average of four judge-based dimensions and excludes the objective metrics, yet it is used to declare an overall winner.

The metric-independence analysis is not sound evidence of orthogonality. Subtracting each sample's mean across metrics mechanically induces negative correlations, visible throughout Figure 9, so low pairwise correlations after this transformation cannot establish that the metrics provide independent information.

Statistical reporting is inadequate for the scale and stochasticity of the study. The paper apparently evaluates one generation per prompt, reports no generation seeds or repeat generations, gives no confidence intervals or significance tests, and does not state model-specific sample counts after proprietary safety failures. Claims such as significantly greater diversity, monotonic difficulty effects, and close leaderboard differences are therefore not adequately supported.

Reproducibility is currently insufficient. The code/data availability sentence contains a blank link, exact proprietary model/API snapshots and generation dates are missing, many inference parameters are described only as native defaults, and the released-evaluator claim is prospective. The robustness experiment ambiguously refers to only 500 video samples rather than the full model-by-prompt collection, and its detailed per-run results are not provided.

Dataset construction and ethics need stronger documentation. Human refinement, checklist verification, annotator training, compensation, demographics, and quality-control outcomes are mostly unspecified. The benchmark uses community prompts and YouTube clips containing possible faces, speech, and copyrighted content, but licensing, consent, privacy, redistribution, and takedown procedures are not discussed. The impact statement mentions misinformation broadly but does not address these dataset-governance issues.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the contribution primarily combines established metrics, an MLLM judge, and a taxonomy-driven prompt suite, while contemporaneous T2AV benchmarks already cover many related dimensions. The claimed first comprehensive benchmark is not convincingly distinguished experimentally from VABench, JavisBench, and related work.

There are several presentation errors that reduce confidence, including lower-is-better L1 columns marked with upward arrows, duplicated or inconsistent table numbering, a duplicated/mislabeled dataset-statistics figure, malformed availability text, and recurring typography/spacing problems. These are secondary to the methodological issues but should be corrected.

strengths: Significance: Evaluating joint text-to-audio-video generation is timely, and the benchmark covers useful dimensions often treated separately: visual/audio quality, cross-modal alignment, instruction following, and perceptual realism.

Scope: The evaluation includes 15 systems spanning proprietary, open-source, end-to-end, and cascaded pipelines. The fine-grained tables expose informative differences that a single leaderboard score would hide.

Diagnostic design: The taxonomy and checklist decomposition are reasonably interpretable, and the analyses of subject count, event complexity, audiovisual synergy, and audio failure types could help identify model failure modes.

Validation effort: The paper includes human ratings, pairwise comparisons, repeated judge runs, preprocessing sensitivity tests, metric-correlation analysis, and a real-video calibration set. The limitations section also appropriately acknowledges judge bias, version drift, computational cost, and limited long-tail coverage.
Presentation: The main narrative and taxonomy are generally understandable, with extensive appendices containing rubrics, prompts, metric definitions, and fine-grained results.
weaknesses: Soundness: The cross-model comparison is materially confounded. Models use different native resolutions, including 480p for Javis, mostly 720p, and 1080p for Kling, while technical/aesthetic quality is directly compared. More seriously, prompts are paraphrased only for Ovi-1.1 and composed pipelines. These interventions change both task difficulty and metric inputs, so the reported rankings cannot be interpreted as controlled comparisons.

Soundness: The central MLLM evaluation is insufficiently validated for the claims made. Gemini-2.5-Pro disagrees with human consensus by 1.420 points on the 1–5 audio-realism scale, 36.3% worse than the reported inter-human baseline, yet the headline conclusion is an “Audio Realism Bottleneck.” Sampling video at only 2 FPS is also questionable for motion smoothness, object permanence, and fine temporal synchronization.

Soundness: The human-study accounting is internally unclear. The paper says five annotators independently rated 250 samples, which would yield far more than the reported 503 annotator pairs per dimension. It then reports N=500 for instruction-following agreement despite having 250 generated samples. The claimed MLLM preservation of human pairwise ordering is not accompanied by the corresponding MLLM head-to-head matrix or ranking in the appendix.

Statistical evidence: Results appear to use one generation per prompt/model, with no repeated generation seeds, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or uncertainty on leaderboard differences. Several leading averages differ by only a few points. Failed generations from closed systems are acknowledged but their frequency and treatment are not reported, potentially biasing comparisons.

Metric validity: Several metrics and aggregation choices are under-specified or weakly justified. The paper does not adequately define the PQ/CU estimators behind Audio Aesthetic Score, gives limited validation for most objective metrics, and averages heterogeneous subjective dimensions into a headline score without establishing calibration or appropriate weighting. The metric-independence de-meaning procedure is unusual and not sufficiently justified.

Benchmark validity: The 400 rewritten prompts are deliberately expanded by Gemini from roughly 54 to 154 tokens, making complexity partly synthetic rather than representative of user requests. The diversity claim relies on an unclear “semantic retention” or embedding-similarity analysis; the manuscript even suggests higher similarity indicates broader coverage, which is not generally true without a precise definition. Only 100 prompts are grounded in real videos.

Judge bias: Gemini is used to rewrite prompts, caption real videos, construct checklist questions, and perform the main judging. This creates correlated model-specific biases that same-family Gemini robustness checks cannot resolve. Restricting checklist questions to expected “Yes” answers also invites affirmative bias and inadequately tests hallucinated or unwanted content.

Originality: The contribution mainly packages existing perceptual metrics, embedding similarities, synchronization models, and MLLM checklist judging into a new dataset. The taxonomy and scale are useful, but the methodological novelty is incremental relative to the several contemporary audiovisual benchmarks discussed in Table 1.

Reproducibility: The manuscript's code/data sentence contains missing links. Critical generation details are absent, including exact API/model versions, access dates, seeds, durations, failure-handling rules, decoding parameters for generators, complete preprocessing, and sufficient configuration details for proprietary systems. Depending on closed Gemini variants further exposes results to vendor drift.

Presentation: Some claims overreach the evidence, including “first comprehensive benchmark,” causal-sounding bottleneck interpretations, and statements that calibration “proves” judge sensitivity. There are also labeling inconsistencies such as T2AVBench versus T2AV-Compass and unclear metric scales, while several dense figures are difficult to read.

Ethics and data governance: The impact statement mentions misinformation, but the paper does not adequately address copyright, consent, privacy, licensing, or redistribution conditions for YouTube clips and community prompts. The filtering diagram mentions NSFW filtering, but its procedure and handling of demographic or cultural bias are not documented.

strengths: [Significance and originality] T2AV-Compass addresses an important, underdeveloped problem with a comparatively broad benchmark: 500 complex prompts, a fine-grained audiovisual taxonomy, 13 reported metrics, and evaluations of 15 end-to-end and cascaded systems. Combining signal-level measures with checklist-based instruction-following and realism diagnostics is useful and more informative than a single aggregate score.

[Soundness] The evaluation is unusually extensive for this emerging setting. Supporting checks include five-annotator human studies, synchronization-metric validation (SRCC 0.9172 against mean human scores), three repeated judge runs, pairwise model comparisons, preprocessing-sensitivity tests, and calibration using 100 real videos.

[Empirical value] The paper produces actionable findings rather than only a leaderboard. The degradation with subject/event complexity, weaknesses on dynamics and sound effects, and comparison of native versus cascaded generation are informative for future model development.

[Presentation and reproducibility] The manuscript is generally well organized and visually polished. Its appendices provide taxonomies, scoring formulas, judge prompts, preprocessing settings, detailed per-dimension results, and dataset-construction procedures.

[Limitations and ethics] The authors candidly acknowledge judge cost, model bias, closed-source dependence, version drift, and incomplete long-tail coverage. The impact statement also recognizes misuse and misinformation risks without overstating the benchmark as a complete safety solution.
weaknesses: [Soundness] The central MLLM evaluation is not equally reliable across dimensions. Gemini-2.5-Pro's audio-realism disagreement is 1.420 on the five-point scale, 36.3% worse than the inter-human value of 1.042. Because the highlighted 'audio realism bottleneck' depends substantially on this dimension, stronger human confirmation and uncertainty estimates are needed.

[Experimental comparability] Systems are evaluated at different native resolutions (480p, mostly 720p, and 1080p), while prompts are paraphrased only for Ovi-1.1 and composed systems. These choices can materially affect quality and instruction-following scores, weakening the fairness of direct rankings. Failed generations from closed systems are mentioned without reporting failure rates or explaining their treatment.

[Statistical evidence] The leaderboard gives point estimates without confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated generations. Claims such as 'significantly outperforming' other datasets in semantic diversity are therefore not established statistically, and rankings separated by small margins may not be robust.

[Validation reporting] Important protocol details are unclear or internally difficult to reconcile. Five annotators allegedly rated 250 samples independently, yet only 503 valid annotator pairs per dimension are reported. The 50-prompt subset is called both Consistency50 and Arena50, and the claimed agreement between Gemini and the human Bradley-Terry ordering is not accompanied by the corresponding Gemini ranking or a quantitative rank-agreement result.

[Metric validity] Most objective and judge-based dimensions receive limited task-specific human calibration; synchronization is the notable exception. Evaluating temporal coherence from 2-FPS frame sampling is questionable, while embedding similarities may miss event-level correspondence. The metric-correlation analysis demonstrates non-redundancy but not validity.

[Reproducibility and ethics] The submitted version contains incomplete code/data links, and core evaluations depend on mutable proprietary models and APIs. The paper also does not adequately document API versions, generation seeds, all model settings, or licensing, consent, and privacy considerations for YouTube clips and community-sourced prompts. Several presentation errors—such as upward arrows for an L1 distance explicitly defined as lower-is-better—should also be corrected.
